chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Dickie Wells from Cecil Scott's Springfield band; his odd trombone style
summary: Wells came from Cecil and Lloyd Scott's band near Wilberforce, played high slides to low notes, and wrote Horace about recording Fletcher's library.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Dickie Wells. There's another great guy, as a person and a musician -- great trombonist. I first met Dickie Wells when I was going to school in Ohio. What was -- in fact, he was one of the original members of a band out of Springfield, Ohio, just a short distance from Wilberforce, and there were two brothers that owned this particular band, and he played in -- and they were Cecil and Lloyd Scott. Cecil Scott was the leader of the band, and Lloyd Scott was -- I think he was the drummer. And Cecil played tenor saxophone and clarinet a la Ted Lewis --
-- he'd have the cape on and the --

-- high hat and all (inaudible), and they went that, -- but they had some great musicians in that band, if I remember correctly. They had a piano player that has been playing in the Village, down in the Village in New York a long time, named Don Frye. He was one of the original bands. I don't know if they call themselves The Syncopaters or not. I forgot, but they're out of -- they were out of Springfield, Ohio. Lloyd Scott was a drummer, and Cecil Scott was a saxophonist. They had an alto player that was later in my big band at Dunbar Palace College named John Williams. He was in that band.

They had a great trumpet player with them. They and you know him, (Bill Coleman - ed.) later went to Europe, (Inaudible) Johnson, Coleman Johnson, excellent trumpet player. He went to Europe. In fact, I think he's still in Europe. Then they had another trumpet player that took his place, great big guy. I know you know this guy's name. I'll get it back to you. But getting back to that band, Dickie Wells was in that group, and he always played a real weird style of trombone.

Well, high, you know -- whoo-oo-o! (imitates trombone) He'd slide, you know, up to it. (Inaudible) and dropped down to low notes, to low with the range, you know? He had that. And nobody else played like that. And he went to New York, and he kind of upset everybody playing like that. In fact, he did a good job because he's still playing in New York, and he's played a lot of the name bands, and I got a letter from Dickie Wells -- it's been quite a few years now; he wrote me and wanted to know if I had my brother's library. He thought it was a great thing before Rex Stewart passed and did this particular thing that I'm talking about. He wanted to revise some of the things and record them, my brother's library that I have. I've got the letter from Dickie. And he Thought it would be a nice thing, he said, because you know all the guys, and a lot of them are living now, and I think we should do it.
You know? But you have to come to New York, one of these kind of things, and I was tied up then, couldn't do it. But it was -- I got the trumpet player's name. Frankie Newton.
